newsitem.title: FINLAND: PSP'S AALTONEN PUTS EVEN ODDS ON NARROW, BROAD EMU.
newsitem.headline: PSP'S AALTONEN PUTS EVEN ODDS ON NARROW, BROAD EMU.

text.p: European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is about as likely to start with just a few nations as with a greater number while the chance of delay is at most 20 percent, a senior Finnish market economist said on Monday.

"Let's say narrow EMU -- 40 percent chance, broad EMU -- 40 percent, and the chance of a delay at most 20 percent," state-owned commercial bank Postipankki's head of treasury and former chief economist Ari Aaltonen told Reuters.
"The political elite in Germany and France is ... committed to this, and so I think the chance of a delay is rather slim," he said in connection with an EMU-seminar hosted by the bank.
A narrow EMU, a model enjoying strong support from a Germany concerned with price stability, would likely include Germany, France, the Benelux countries, Austria and Finland, Aaltonen said.
A broader EMU, which has the backing of France which is eager to pin down exchange rates, would also include some or all of the southern European countries, he said.
"If EMU gets started, Finland will be part of it," he said.
If the launch of EMU were to be delayed beyond the scheduled January 1, 1999, start-up date, it would not be a major shock to Finnish interest rates, Aaltonen said.

"I don't think (a delay of EMU) would have more than a temporary effect on Finland because German interest rates would fall," he said, adding that German long rates could fall by half a percentage point in case of a postponement.
"Our interest rate gap (to Germany) would grow, but in absolute terms we would stay at about the current level," he said.
"The spread would grow sharply at first, but in absolute terms a delay wouldn't cause any big upset," he said.

The risk Finland took by pegging the markka to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) as late as mid-October 1996 could grow increasingly important if EMU candidates start to argue fiercely over Italian EMU membership, Aaltonen said.
If other EMU candidates were to decide to drop Italy out of monetary union, they might argue that Italy had not been inside the ERM for the required two-year period, Aaltonen said.
In that case, Finland's ERM membership of just barely two years ahead of the EMU start-up could become more of a risk, he said.

If Finland joined EMU, Aaltonen said he expected the markka to be converted into the new single currency, the euro, close to the same central parity exchange rate at which it was linked to Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in October 1996, or around 3.04 markka per German mark.
